top_story: Israel’s 7 May strike on Beirut, the first on the Lebanese capital since last month’s ceasefire with Hezbollah, signals a sharp erosion of already fragile de-escalation and raises the risk that Lebanon will again absorb the costs of regional confrontation through damage to urban infrastructure and renewed civilian insecurity. That pressure is unfolding in a wider environment shaped since March by Tehran’s increasingly secretive execution campaign, which points to a regime hardening internally as it manages dissent under blackout conditions and limits the space for public reaction. Since Trump’s 23 March threat against Iran’s power grid and demand tied to the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian officials have framed confrontation as regional rather than bilateral, making spillover across Lebanon and other arenas more plausible. The emerging picture is of simultaneous external escalation and internal repression reinforcing each other, narrowing off-ramps and increasing the likelihood that civilians will bear the immediate consequences.
